title: Predictive–Generative Drift Decomposition for Speech Enhancement and Separation
claim: A pretrained predictor's drift and a clean-speech denoiser's noise estimate combine in an iterative sampling loop to produce the output.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, dashed box with feedback loop around sampling step
description: A single wide block diagram reads left to right. Input y enters a peach rounded box labeled P_phi, outside a dashed rounded rectangle titled 'Sampling with SIPS'. P_phi's output, labeled v-hat, runs as a long arrow into a large gray box inside the dashed region, 'Sampling Step cf. Eq. (7)'. A small light-blue box D_theta sits above and to the left. It sends z-hat down into the sampling step. The sampling step's output exits right as s-hat. A branch of that output loops back along the top as x_t, feeding both D_theta and the sampling step. Colors are pastel, lines are black, and labels are italic math. The eye goes first to the large central sampling box.
caption: Overview of the proposed plug-and-play framework. The predictor $P_\phi$ defines a deterministic drift $\hat{v} = P_\phi(y) - y$ from the observation $y$, while the denoiser $D_\theta$ estimates the Gaussian noise component $\hat{z}$ to incorporate the learned clean speech prior. Both components are combined in each sampling step to update the current state $x_t$, ultimately yielding the final clean speech estimate $\hat{s}$.
abstract: We propose Stochastic Interpolant Prior for Speech (SIPS), a plug-and-play framework for speech enhancement and separation that augments pretrained predictors with a generative clean speech prior. Building on stochastic interpolants, we decompose the sampling dynamics into a predictor-induced drift and a score-based denoising component. The predictor guides sampling toward a task-consistent estimate, while a score model trained exclusively on clean speech promotes perceptual naturalness. Unlike prior hybrid approaches, which typically rely on architecture-specific conditioning and are tied to particular predictors or degradation settings, SIPS employs a degradation-agnostic prior that can be reused across predictors and additive degradation tasks without retraining. We evaluate SIPS on speech enhancement and separation using recent predictors such as SEMamba and FlexIO. Across both tasks, SIPS consistently improves non-intrusive speech quality metrics while maintaining competitive performance on reference-based distortion measures and word error rate. For speech enhancement, these improvements are further supported by a subjective listening test.
